title: Morning stiffness and frailty: a slower start that still starts (UK)
meta_title: Morning stiffness and frailty: a slower start that still starts
meta_description: Practical morning routines when arthritis stiffness and frailty make getting up hard, plus when long morning stiffness may need a medical review.
excerpt: Practical morning routines when arthritis stiffness and frailty make getting up hard, plus when long morning stiffness may need a medical review.
direct_answer: Morning stiffness is common in arthritis. In osteoarthritis, it usually eases within 30 minutes. Stiffness lasting longer may suggest inflammatory arthritis or polymyalgia rheumatica and should be checked. A slower, planned start with gentle movement, warmth and rest helps.
author: Louis Maxwell
reviewer_credentials: First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483, CSP member
keywords: morning stiffness, arthritis, frailty, morning routine, inflammatory arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, UK
content:
Many people with arthritis find mornings the hardest part of the day. With frailty, getting going can take even longer.

This guide offers ideas for a gentler start. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Before getting up

  • Gentle stretches in bed, such as ankle circles and knee bends.
  • Take pain relief at a time that suits you, as advised.
  • Sit on the edge of the bed for a moment before standing.

A slower start

  • A warm shower or bath can ease stiffness.
  • Lay clothes out the night before.
  • Use dressing aids.
  • Allow extra time so you are not rushed.

When to get it checked

Tell your GP if stiffness lasts more than 30 to 60 minutes, comes with swollen joints, or is new and affects shoulders and hips. These may be signs of inflammatory arthritis or polymyalgia rheumatica.

Keeping active

Regular activity during the day can reduce stiffness over time.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Why are mornings worse?

Joints stiffen after periods of not moving.

Should I rest more?

Gentle movement usually helps more than rest.
